situation.note: we lost the baby at 11 weeks. everyone says it's common and at least it was early. I don't know why that makes it worse.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call missing someone you love, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: From being told to be grateful for a loss to letting the love that was real have its full place, without apology.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the grief as real and the loneliness as real, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the love was real and the loss was real, and that no one else's comfort can change that.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be taken away.
week_beats.act: You try letting the grief move without forcing gratitude, and speaking the true thing about what was lost.
week_beats.story: A mother who lost her child early shows you what it means to stand in the truth of your love.

understanding.core_struggle: Lost a baby at eleven weeks, and the words meant to comfort her are making the grief feel heavier and more alone.
understanding.mirror: At eleven weeks, and the world tells you it was early, as if early makes it smaller.
understanding.insight: You are grieving something that was yours and real. The comfort that doesn't fit is the part that hurts most.

queries.hook: I'm grieving someone I loved. Inside, my mind won't settle, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: Grief is love with nowhere to go; the more the bond was real, the deeper the ache when it is taken away, and no one else can give it back.
queries.steady: What is real in us cannot be lost, even when what we loved is taken away; the love remains and so does the ache.
queries.act: Let the love have its place, speak the true thing about what was lost, and let the grief move without forcing it to be grateful.
queries.story: A mother who lost her child early, surrounded by those who could not see her pain, who found her footing in the truth of what she had loved.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

matched.label: I can't focus, my mind is restless

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says holding it feels like holding the wind. Krishna answers that the mind is indeed hard to hold, but practice and letting go can train it.
verse.for_you: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind. You sit in this quiet, and the words of others land like stones. You do not need to steady the wind today.
asks: How do I hold the wind without fighting it?
How do I make the storm of my mind feel less alone?

verse.speaker: Kausalya
verse.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
verse.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
verse.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
verse.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
verse.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

verse.meaning: Kausalya, the mother of Rama, has just shouted at her husband Dasharatha for sending their son away. She sees him fold his hands and ask her forgiveness. She is horrified that grief made her wound the man she loves. She tells him that grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it. She explains that grief destroys everything. The verse proposes that when sorrow makes you lash out at the people you love, an apology heals faster than being right.
verse.for_you: The comfort people offered you was meant to steady you, but it only wounded you more. Grief is wearing away your steadiness and your judgement right now. The love you lost was real and the loss was real. Let the love you had have its full place, without apology.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when a kind word feels like a wound.
verse.scene_line: You are Kausalya after the grief has passed, seeing how sorrow wounded the people you love.
asks: How do I tell my grief it is allowed to be this loud?
How do I stop my mind from turning comfort into a wound?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.sanskrit: वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहायनवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि । तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
verse.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.
verse.misuse: Not a way to brush off someone else's grief with 'they've just changed clothes'.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna, who is drowning in sorrow on the battlefield. He says that just as a person discards old, worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self leaves behind a worn-out body and enters a new one. The point is that your real self outlasts every loss and every passing pain. The body is just a garment that is shed, while what is truly you remains.
verse.for_you: The grief you are holding is heavy because it is real, and that reality is yours. The words of others do not change the fact that you loved something that existed. Your core self is not the pain.
verse.try_today: Let yourself feel the weight of the loss without trying to push it away.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
verse.sanskrit: नायमत्यन्तसंवासो लभ्यते जातु केनचित् / अपि स्वेन शरीरेण किमुतान्येन केनचित्
verse.line: No one gets to stay with anyone forever, not even with their own body.
verse.translation: No one ever gets to live together with anyone forever, not even with one's own body, let alone with anyone else.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the sage Ashma how to bear the loss of family and wealth. Ashma tells him that no one ever gets to live together with anyone forever, not even with their own body, let alone with anyone else. The idea is that days do not come back, and meetings end. Grieve, and then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
verse.for_you: You are holding a loss that others call common, and that makes the silence around you louder. The love you had was real, and it does not shrink because someone else says it should. What you feel is not a mistake. Hold on to the truth of it.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing you still hold in your hands today.
verse.scene_line: You stand where a king once stood, asking how to bear a loss no one else will name.
asks: How do I hold the love without the body?
Who steadies me when my own mind is the storm?

verse.speaker: Narada
verse.setting: Narada to Shuka on troubles that affect many people at once.
verse.sanskrit: न जानपदिकं दुःखमेकः शोचितुमर्हति / अशोचन्प्रतिकुर्वीत यदि पश्येदुपक्रमम्
verse.line: Don't just grieve over a problem everyone faces. If you see a way to fix it, act.
verse.translation: No one should sit alone grieving over a trouble that has struck everyone. Instead of grieving, act to remedy it if you see a way.
verse.why: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

prasang.title: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

verse.meaning: Narada speaks to Shuka, who is young and turning away from the world. Shuka is grieving the loss of his father and feels overwhelmed by sorrow. Narada tells him not to sit alone in his grief, because a problem shared and addressed is less heavy than one held in silence. He says that if you see a way to fix something, you could act on it. He is not telling Shuka to stop missing his father. He is saying that grief that only circles in the mind grows like a wound left open.
verse.for_you: You are holding a loss that others keep trying to shrink, and that makes the weight feel heavier. The comfort that does not fit is the part that hurts most. You do not need to force gratitude for what was lost.
verse.try_today: Let the grief move without forcing gratitude, and speak the true thing about what was lost.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own quiet room, facing a trouble that has struck your own heart.
asks: How do I tend to a mind that is sick without pretending it is well?
Can sorrow be a thing I care for rather than a thing I fight?

verse.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
verse.setting: The sage to the ruined prince Kshemadarshi, who keeps longing for what he lost.
verse.line: Want what is within reach. Enjoy what is here now. Don't grieve over what hasn't happened.
verse.translation: Wish for what can be had, never for what cannot. Enjoy what is in front of you now, and do not grieve over what has not yet come.
verse.why: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

prasang.title: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

verse.for_you: Let yourself grieve, honour them by living well, and remember that the self they loved in you, and in them, does not perish.

story.title: Sumitra sits with Kausalya
story.story_hook: Two mothers, two sons gone to the same forest, and one of them found the strength to comfort the other.
story.summary: Kausalya weeps for her son gone to the forest. Her co-queen Sumitra, whose own son has gone too, comforts her: he went for a good reason, he is not alone, and you will see him again.
story.lesson: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.

anchor.speaker: Sumitra
anchor.setting: Ram has left for fourteen years; his mother cannot stop weeping, and her co-queen sits with her.
anchor.sanskrit: निवृत्तवनवासं तं द्रष्टासि पुनरागतम्। जहि शोकं च मोहं च देवि सत्यं ब्रवीमि ते॥
anchor.line: You will see him again. Let go of this grief.
anchor.translation: You will see him again, back from the forest. Let go of grief and confusion, my queen. I tell you the truth.
anchor.why: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.
anchor.misuse: Comfort for a long separation, not a promise that every loss will be undone.

prasang.title: Sumitra sits with Kausalya
prasang.summary: Kausalya weeps for her son gone to the forest. Her co-queen Sumitra, whose own son has gone too, comforts her: he went for a good reason, he is not alone, and you will see him again.
prasang.story_hook: Two mothers, two sons gone to the same forest, and one of them found the strength to comfort the other.
prasang.lesson: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.

story.hook_title: Both their sons were gone, and Sumitra found the strength to comfort Kausalya
story.teaser: Both their sons were gone, and Sumitra found the strength to comfort Kausalya
story.for_you: Kausalya's grief was real and raw. Sumitra did not try to fix it with logic. She sat in the shared ache and offered a promise of return. Your family and work may not know the depth of your loss. Let that be.
asks: How can I hold my grief without needing others to name it?
What does it mean to comfort myself when no one else will?
Where does my love live when the body is gone?
